title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 3
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Arms Race We Started
passages.text:
A. Resistance to antibiotics is frequently presented as something bacteria have recently developed in response to human carelessness. The reality is older and stranger. Genes conferring resistance have been recovered from permafrost sediments tens of thousands of years old and from bacteria in caves isolated from the surface for millions of years. Antibiotics are largely compounds that micro-organisms evolved to compete with one another, and defences against them evolved alongside. What human use changed was not the existence of resistance but its abundance.

B. The mechanism by which abundance rises is straightforward and often misdescribed. An antibiotic does not cause bacteria to become resistant. It kills those that are susceptible, leaving those that already carry a resistance trait to multiply without competition. Selection, not adaptation, does the work. This distinction matters practically: it means the speed at which resistance spreads depends on how much of the population is exposed and for how long, rather than on any property of the individual bacterium's response.

C. Bacteria also acquire resistance in a way that has no equivalent in animals. Genes can move directly between organisms, including between different species, carried on small circular fragments of DNA. A resistance trait that arises in a harmless soil bacterium can therefore appear in a dangerous human pathogen without any shared ancestry. This is why resistance in agricultural settings is a human health question rather than a separate agricultural one.

D. Agricultural use accounts for a large share of total antibiotic consumption in many countries, much of it not for treating illness but for growth promotion and routine disease prevention in crowded conditions. The practice is economically rational for an individual producer and collectively destructive, which is the classic shape of a problem no single participant can solve alone. Several jurisdictions have restricted growth-promotion use, and where restrictions were imposed, resistance in the relevant bacteria has in some cases measurably declined.

E. The pipeline of new drugs is the part of the problem least amenable to public pressure. Developing an antibiotic is expensive and the resulting product is one that doctors are instructed to use as little as possible, for short courses, and to hold in reserve. A drug that succeeds medically therefore fails commercially by design, and most large manufacturers have withdrawn from the field. The shortage is not scientific in origin; it is a consequence of how the incentive is arranged.

F. Proposals to fix that incentive share a common structure: they separate payment from volume sold. Governments would pay a fixed sum for access to a new antibiotic regardless of how many courses are prescribed, in effect purchasing availability rather than doses. Pilot schemes exist and are small. Whether they scale is the open question, and it is a question about public finance rather than about microbiology.

passages.title: Counting on Bees
passages.text:
A substantial proportion of the crops humans eat depend on animal pollination, and the figure is regularly misquoted in both directions. It is not true that most of the world's food supply depends on bees: the staple cereals that supply the bulk of human calories — wheat, rice, maize — are wind-pollinated or self-pollinating and would be unaffected. It is true that a large share of the crops supplying vitamins, minerals and dietary variety are animal-pollinated, so the consequence of pollinator loss falls on nutritional quality more than on caloric quantity.

The honey bee dominates public discussion and is not the species most at risk. It is a managed, farmed animal, kept in hives, moved by lorry and replaced when colonies fail. Its numbers globally have risen over recent decades, because beekeepers respond to losses by splitting surviving colonies. Reporting that treats honey bee colony losses as evidence of a collapse in pollinators generally has the situation almost exactly backwards: the farmed species is the one with a manager whose interest is its survival.

Wild pollinators are the genuine concern and the harder problem. Solitary bees, bumblebees, hoverflies, beetles and moths pollinate extensively, often more efficiently per visit than honey bees, and several crops are pollinated better by wild species even where managed hives are present. These populations have no keeper. Their decline is driven by habitat loss, the simplification of landscapes into large single-crop fields, pesticide exposure and reduced flowering across the season — and, unlike a hive, they cannot be replaced by splitting.

The commercial pollination industry has grown into the gap and has introduced a risk of its own. Hives are transported across continents to arrive as crops flower, concentrating enormous numbers of bees in one place for a few weeks. This is efficient and it is also an ideal arrangement for transmitting parasites and pathogens between colonies that would never otherwise meet, and from managed bees into wild populations nearby. The practice that compensates for pollinator scarcity contributes to it.

What follows from this is a shift in what counts as a solution. Keeping more honey bees addresses a shortage of managed pollination and does little for the underlying problem; in some settings it competes with wild species for forage. Interventions with better evidence are unglamorous: uncultivated field margins, hedgerows, staggered flowering so that forage exists across the whole season rather than in a single flush, and reduced pesticide exposure at the times pollinators are active. None of these produces a photograph of a beehive, which is a poor reason for their comparative neglect in public campaigns.

passages.title: Reading the Unreadable
passages.text:
A script that no living person can read presents a problem with a structure unlike most historical questions, because success is verifiable. Either the proposed readings produce sensible text across new material or they do not, and the discipline has a clear record of both outcomes.

Decipherment almost always requires one of two advantages. The first is a bilingual text — the same content in a known script and the unknown one — which converts the problem from invention into comparison. The second is a known underlying language written in an unfamiliar script, which allows the decipherer to test proposed sound values against words they already expect to find. Where neither is available, the record of success is poor, and several scripts have resisted more than a century of competent effort for precisely this reason.

The best-documented decipherment illustrates the method. A Bronze Age script from the Aegean was assumed for decades to record an unknown language unrelated to Greek, an assumption held by the scholars best placed to judge. The breakthrough came from an amateur who set the assumption aside and built grids showing which symbols shared consonants and which shared vowels, without assigning sound values at all. The grid was a structural argument, and only once it was stable did values follow — at which point the language proved to be an early form of Greek, which almost nobody had expected.

Two lessons are usually drawn and only one survives scrutiny. The popular lesson, that outsiders see what specialists cannot, is weakly supported: most amateur decipherment claims are wrong, and the successful case succeeded because its author did rigorous structural work, not because he was an outsider. The durable lesson concerns assumptions. The field had been anchored to a belief about the language that was never evidence-based, and progress required suspending it rather than arguing against it.

Statistical methods have changed what is possible without changing the fundamental constraint. Computational analysis can establish the number of distinct signs — which distinguishes an alphabet from a syllabary from a system of word-signs — and can identify repeated sequences that behave like grammatical endings. What it cannot do is supply meaning. A system whose underlying language has no known relative remains resistant, because there is nothing to test a proposal against, and no amount of computation creates that.

The most-discussed undeciphered script has resisted for over a century despite abundant inscriptions, and the reason is instructive: the inscriptions are almost all extremely short, no bilingual has been found, and the language is unknown. Each of those conditions alone is difficult; together they may be decisive, and a growing number of specialists argue that decipherment may not be achievable with the material currently available — a conclusion that is unsatisfying, well-evidenced and correspondingly unpopular.
